name: Map the world's vegetation every month
summary: Farmers and scientists want a fresh map of plant health for all land on Earth, every month.
objective: Measure plant health over all land once a month. Healthy plants absorb red light and reflect near-infrared light, so the camera must record both.

requirements.label: See every place at least once every 30 days
requirements.why_it_matters: A monthly map needs a new picture of every place each month. A camera with a narrow view takes longer to cover the Earth.

requirements.label: Show details 30 m across or smaller
requirements.why_it_matters: Each pixel of the picture covers a square of ground. Smaller pixels show smaller fields and forest patches. Flying higher makes each pixel cover more ground.

requirements.label: Send at least 500 GB of pictures to the ground each month
requirements.why_it_matters: Pictures are only useful once they reach the ground. The radio and the ground stations set how much data gets down.

requirements.label: Keep working for at least 2 years
requirements.why_it_matters: Plant health changes with the seasons, so the maps must cover more than one year. Low orbits decay sooner because of air drag.

real_mission_fact: NASA's Landsat 9 flies 705 km up and photographs each place every 16 days. Its main camera shows details 30 m across in a strip of ground 185 km wide.
estimate_basis: The 30 m threshold matches Landsat 9's main camera. The 30-day revisit, 2-year lifetime and US$10 million budget are game-design values. The 500 GB threshold is derived: one map of all land (148.94 million km2) in two bands (red and near-infrared) at 30 m pixels and 12 bits per pixel, uncompressed, is 496 GB, rounded to 500. All thresholds will be re-tuned once the simulation exists.
